read.sections.0.heading.source: A thing can connect several places
read.sections.0.heading.back: One thing can connect several places

read.sections.0.text.source:
Objects can connect distant societies through making, transport, exchange and use. Ceramics, or objects made of fired clay, are useful evidence. Fired clay survives well, and vessels were made in large numbers. Their histories connect artistic decisions with workshops, ships and people's demand for goods. Southeast Asian makers took an active part in these networks.

A Vietnamese dish in The Metropolitan Museum of Art shows a bird flying among clouds. It is dated to the early sixteenth century. The museum says it was probably made in Hai D'uong Province. This is an attribution, a reasoned identification of where it was made. The bird is painted in cobalt blue under a transparent glaze, a glass-like coating. The free brushwork shows a practised skill in decorating many vessels.

The dish was recovered from the cargo of the Hoi An shipwreck, near central Vietnam. The cargo was found in the late 1990s. It showed how large Vietnamese production of glazed ceramics had been.
read.sections.0.text.back:
Objects can connect societies far apart through making, transport, exchange and use. Ceramics, that is objects of fired clay, are useful evidence. Fired clay lasts a long time, and vessels were made in large numbers. The history of ceramics connects artistic decisions with workshops, ships and people's demand for goods. Makers in Southeast Asia took an active part in these networks.

A Vietnamese dish in The Metropolitan Museum of Art shows a bird flying among clouds. This dish is dated to the early 16th century. The museum says this dish was probably made in Hai D'uong Province. This is an attribution, that is a reasoned identification of the place it was made. The bird is painted with cobalt blue under a transparent glaze, that is a glass-like layer. The free brushstrokes show a practised skill in decorating many vessels.

The dish was found in the cargo of the Hoi An shipwreck, near the middle part of Vietnam. The cargo was found in the late 1990s. It showed how big the production of glazed ceramics in Vietnam was.
read.sections.0.text.note: "Attribution" is "atribusi", the museum term; reviewer to say whether learners will know it (the reading explains it). "Cargo" is "kargo".

read.sections.0.simpler.source:
Objects can link places that are far apart. People make them, carry them, trade them and use them. Ceramics are things made of baked clay. They are good evidence. Baked clay lasts a long time. And people made very many of them. Makers in Southeast Asia played a big part in this trade.

A dish in a museum in New York shows a bird in clouds. It is from the early 1500s. The museum says it was probably made in Hai D'uong, in Vietnam. This is an attribution. It is a careful, reasoned idea of where it was made. The bird is painted in blue under a clear glaze. A glaze is a shiny coat, like glass. The quick brush lines show a skilled hand.

The dish was in the cargo of a ship that sank near Hoi An. Cargo means goods carried together. The wreck was found in the late 1990s. It showed that Vietnam made a huge number of glazed dishes.
read.sections.0.simpler.back:
Objects can connect places that are far apart. People make them, carry them, sell them and use them. Ceramics are things made of fired clay. Ceramics are good evidence. Fired clay lasts a long time. People also made very many ceramics. Makers in Southeast Asia played a big part in this trade.

A dish in a museum in New York shows a bird in clouds. It is from the early 1500s. The museum says it was probably made in Hai D'uong, in Vietnam. This is an attribution. It is a careful and reasoned idea of where it was made. The bird is painted in blue under a clear glaze. A glaze is a shiny layer, like glass. The quick brush lines show a skilled hand.

The dish was in the cargo of a ship that sank near Hoi An. Cargo means goods carried together. The shipwreck was found in the late 1990s. It showed that Vietnam made very many glazed dishes.

read.sections.1.text.source:
The dish was part of a regional economy. The Met records fifteenth- and sixteenth-century Vietnamese ceramics made for use at home and for export. Indonesia was a market for Chinese and Southeast Asian wares. Vietnamese makers produced vessels shaped like animals as well as dishes. They also made tiles used on Indonesian mosques and other buildings. Exchange connected objects for the home, decoration on buildings and religious settings. But this pattern does not tell us who bought the pictured dish, or where it was going.

Making ceramics also had a local history. Under the early Lê dynasty, in the fifteenth century, policies encouraged industry and trade. Specialised craft communities supplied different customers. The Vietnam National Museum of History names Bát Tràng, near Hanoi, and Nam Sách in Hải Dương as important centres for blue-and-white ceramics. Makers there supplied everyday vessels and special forms for buyers at home and overseas. So Vietnam was a place where people organised production and made choices. It was not just a stopping point between other societies. Still, this does not prove which kiln, or pottery oven, made this dish.

The dish's materials explain part of how it looks. Cobalt gives the blue decoration, and the clear glaze lets the brushwork show. People in a workshop worked together on shaping, decorating and firing. Making many vessels did not make each person's skill disappear. A workshop joined learned artistic knowledge to the practical work of supplying goods.
read.sections.1.text.back:
The dish was part of a regional economy. The Met records 15th- and 16th-century Vietnamese ceramics made for use within the country and for export. Indonesia was a market for goods from China and Southeast Asia. Vietnamese makers produced vessels shaped like animals as well as dishes. They also made tiles used on mosques and other buildings in Indonesia. Exchange connected objects for the home, decoration on buildings and religious places. But this pattern does not tell us who bought the dish in the picture, or where it was being taken.

The making of ceramics also has a local history. Under the early Lê dynasty, in the 15th century, government policies encouraged industry and trade. Specialised craft communities supplied different customers. The Vietnam National Museum of History names Bát Tràng, near Hanoi, and Nam Sách in Hải Dương as important centres for blue and white ceramics. Makers there supplied everyday vessels and special forms for buyers inside and outside the country. So Vietnam was a place where people organised production and made choices. It was not merely a stopping place between other societies. Still, this does not prove which kiln, that is pottery furnace, made this dish.

The dish's materials explain part of how it looks. Cobalt gives the blue decoration, and the clear glaze lets the brushstrokes be seen. People in a workshop worked together to shape, decorate and fire. Making many vessels did not make each person's skill disappear. A workshop combined learned artistic knowledge with the practical work of supplying goods.
read.sections.1.text.note: "Kiln" is "tanur"; the reading explains it as "relau tembikar" (a pottery furnace). Museum name translated in the reading, kept in English in source labels.

read.sections.1.simpler.source:
Vietnam was part of a big trade area. The Met says Vietnamese makers made pots for home and to sell abroad. Indonesia bought pots from China and Southeast Asia. Vietnamese makers also made pots shaped like animals. They made tiles for mosques and other buildings in Indonesia. But we do not know who bought this dish. We do not know where it was going.

In the 1400s, the Lê rulers of Vietnam helped craft and trade grow. Some places were known for blue-and-white pots. A museum in Hanoi names two: Bát Tràng and Nam Sách. They made pots for people at home and far away. So Vietnamese people planned and chose their own work. Vietnam was not just a stop between other places. But we do not know which oven baked this dish.

The blue paint came from cobalt. The clear glaze lets the brush lines show. In a workshop, people shaped, painted and baked the pots together. They made many pots. But each maker still needed skill.
read.sections.1.simpler.back:
Vietnam was part of a big trade area. According to The Met, Vietnam made pottery for within the country and for abroad. Indonesia bought pottery from China and Southeast Asia. Vietnamese makers also made pottery shaped like animals. They made tiles for mosques and other buildings in Indonesia. But we do not know who bought this dish. We do not know where it was being taken.

In the 1400s, the Lê rulers of Vietnam helped craft and trade grow. Some places were famous for blue and white pottery. A museum in Hanoi names two places: Bát Tràng and Nam Sách. They made pottery for people near and far. So Vietnamese people planned and chose their own work. Vietnam was not merely a stopping place between other places. But we do not know which furnace fired this dish.

The blue paint came from cobalt. The clear glaze lets the brush lines be seen. In a workshop, people shaped, coloured and fired pottery together. They made a lot of pottery. But each maker still needed skill.

read.sections.2.text.source:
A seventeenth-century bronze covered box made in China shows a different connection. Its lid carries an Arabic religious inscription, writing that calls on God's mercy and compassion. The museum places it in the Kangxi period of the Qing dynasty. Chinese making and Arabic religious expression show why a label naming one place cannot describe every relationship in an object. An inscription can be writing and a designed part of a surface at the same time. It does not tell us who used this box, or prove that it was sent abroad.

Exchange was more than goods moving between points on a map. Makers served different uses and audiences. Objects carried designs and religious expressions as well as materials. Particular works reveal these relationships, while parts of their journeys stay uncertain.
read.sections.2.text.back:
A 17th-century bronze box with a lid made in China shows a different connection. Its lid has a religious inscription in Arabic, that is writing that asks for God's mercy and compassion. The museum places it in the Kangxi period, Qing dynasty. Chinese making and Arabic religious expression show why a label naming one place cannot describe every relationship in an object. An inscription can be writing and also a designed part of the surface at the same time. It does not tell us who used this box, or prove that the box was sent abroad.

Exchange was more than goods moving between points on a map. Makers met different uses and audiences. Objects carried designs and religious expressions, and not only materials. Particular works reveal these relationships, although parts of their journeys are still uncertain.
read.sections.2.text.note: "God" is "Tuhan", as in the English and the museum's account; a reviewer may prefer "Allah" for an Arabic Islamic inscription. Don't add a fuller translation of the inscription (educatorNotes.0).

read.sections.2.simpler.source:
A bronze box from China is from the 1600s. It shows a different link. Its lid has writing in Arabic. This writing is an inscription. It asks for God's mercy and kindness. The museum says it was made under the Qing rulers of China. So a box made in China carries Arabic religious words. One place name cannot tell the whole story of an object. The writing is also part of the design. But it does not tell us who used the box. It does not prove the box went abroad.

Trade was more than goods moving on a map. Objects carried designs and beliefs too. They show us links between people. But parts of their journeys stay unknown.
read.sections.2.simpler.back:
A bronze box from China is from the 1600s. It shows a different connection. Its lid has Arabic writing. This writing is an inscription. It asks for God's mercy and loving kindness. The museum says this box was made during the rule of the Qing dynasty in China. So a box made in China carries religious words in Arabic. One place name cannot tell the whole story of an object. The writing is also part of the design. But it does not tell us who used the box. It does not prove the box went abroad.

Trade is more than goods moving on a map. Objects carried designs and beliefs too. They show connections between people. But parts of their journeys are still not known.

write.example.source: The dish shows a connection because it was found in the cargo of a ship that sank near Hoi An. This tells us that Vietnamese makers made many glazed dishes that travelled by sea, and that they were part of a big trade in Southeast Asia. Its record does not tell us who was going to buy it or where the ship was going. We also do not know which kiln made it.
write.example.back: The dish shows a connection because it was found in the cargo of a ship that sank near Hoi An. This tells us that Vietnamese makers made many glazed dishes that were carried by sea, and they were part of a big trade in Southeast Asia. Its record does not tell us who was going to buy it or where the ship was sailing. We also do not know which kiln made it.

educatorNotes.0.source: The box's record doesn't show that it was exported or who used it. Keep its inscription and Chinese origin apart from the dish's evidence from a shipwreck cargo; the two are separate works, not goods from the same cargo. Don't treat every shared colour or motif as proof of direct borrowing, and don't translate the inscription beyond the museum's account (a call on God's mercy and compassion).

Don't treat every shared colour or motif as proof of direct borrowing, and don't translate the inscription beyond the museum's account (asking for God's mercy and compassion).

educatorNotes.2.source: Keep "probably" in the dish's attribution to Hai D'uong Province. The Vietnam National Museum of History article (2015) is used only for how craft was organised under the early Lê dynasty, the centres at Bát Tràng and Nam Sách, and demand at home and overseas; its older shipwreck dating and its identification of a named craftswoman aren't used. It doesn't show which kiln made this dish.
